### Stage: items

## Vragen

### Vraag 1 (5 pt)

Een onderzoeker wil weten hoeveel uur per week eerstejaarsstudenten gemiddeld aan hun studie besteden. Een steekproef van 25 studenten geeft een gemiddelde van 40 uur en een standaarddeviatie van 10 uur.

Gegeven: t* = 2,064 (95%, n = 25).

a. Bereken het 95%-betrouwbaarheidsinterval voor het gemiddelde aantal studie-uren in de populatie. Schrijf je berekening op.
b. Interpreteer het interval in maximaal twee zinnen, in het kader van de onderzoeksvraag.
c. Een collega zegt: "95% van de eerstejaarsstudenten besteedt tussen 35,9 en 44,1 uur per week aan de studie." Leg in maximaal twee zinnen uit of dit klopt.

### Vraag 2 (5 pt)

Een onderzoeker meet bij 25 deelnemers de reactietijd (in milliseconden, ms) op een aandachtstaak. De steekproef geeft een gemiddelde van 130 ms en een standaarddeviatie van 25 ms. Een testhandleiding noemt 115 ms als gemiddelde reactietijd in de populatie.

Gegeven: t* = 2,064 (95%, n = 25).

a. Bereken het 95%-betrouwbaarheidsinterval voor de gemiddelde reactietijd. Schrijf je berekening op.
b. Is 115 ms een waarde voor het populatiegemiddelde die met deze steekproef verenigbaar is? Motiveer je antwoord met het interval, in maximaal twee zinnen.

### Vraag 3 (2 pt)

Een psycholoog meet de ervaren werkdruk (schaal 0 tot 100) van 25 medewerkers van een zorginstelling. Het steekproefgemiddelde is 60 en de standaarddeviatie is 15.

Gegeven: t* = 2,064 (95%, n = 25).

Wat is het 95%-betrouwbaarheidsinterval voor de gemiddelde werkdruk in de populatie?

A. 29,04 tot 90,96
B. 53,81 tot 66,19
C. 57,00 tot 63,00
D. 58,76 tot 61,24

### Vraag 4 (2 pt)

Een onderzoeker laat 25 deelnemers een geheugentest maken. De standaarddeviatie van de scores is 20. Het 95%-betrouwbaarheidsinterval heeft de vorm x̄ ± marge.

Gegeven: t* = 2,064 (95%, n = 25).

Wat is de marge in punten?

A. 1,65
B. 4,00
C. 8,26
D. 41,28

### Vraag 5 (1 pt)

Bij 25 studenten wordt een concentratietest afgenomen. Het steekproefgemiddelde is 52. Het 95%-betrouwbaarheidsinterval voor het gemiddelde loopt van 48 tot 56.

Welke interpretatie van dit interval is juist?

A. Ongeveer 95% van de studenten in de steekproef scoort tussen 48 en 56.
B. Een nieuwe student scoort met 95% kans tussen 48 en 56.
C. Het steekproefgemiddelde ligt met 95% kans tussen 48 en 56.
D. Populatiegemiddelden van 48 tot 56 zijn verenigbaar met de steekproef.

### Vraag 6 (1 pt)

Een onderzoeker berekent een 95%-betrouwbaarheidsinterval voor een gemiddelde.

Welke ene wijziging maakt het interval breder, terwijl al het andere gelijk blijft?

A. De betrouwbaarheid verhogen van 95% naar 99%.
B. De steekproef vergroten van 25 naar 100 deelnemers.
C. De betrouwbaarheid verlagen van 95% naar 90%.
D. Een hoger steekproefgemiddelde vinden.

### Vraag 7 (3 pt)

Een onderzoeker wil weten of mensen die de afgelopen nacht minder dan 6 uur sliepen, gemiddeld langzamer reageren dan mensen die 8 uur sliepen. Er doen 40 deelnemers mee: 20 deelnemers in elke slaapgroep, allemaal verschillende personen. Van iedereen wordt de reactietijd in milliseconden gemeten.

Welke toets is hier passend? Noem de toets, het meetniveau van de afhankelijke variabele en het aantal groepen. Antwoord in maximaal drie zinnen.

### Vraag 8 (3 pt)

Een onderzoeker vraagt 150 eerstejaarsstudenten naar hun woonsituatie (bij ouders, op kamer of anders) en of ze hun eerste studiejaar hebben gehaald (ja of nee). De onderzoeksvraag is of de woonsituatie samenhangt met het halen van het eerste jaar.

Noem de passende toets en motiveer je keuze aan de hand van het meetniveau van de variabelen. Leg ook uit waarom een t-toets hier niet past. Antwoord in maximaal vier zinnen.

### Vraag 9 (2 pt)

Een richtlijn adviseert 8 uur slaap per nacht. Een psycholoog meet bij 30 studenten het aantal uren slaap per nacht. Hij wil weten of het gemiddelde aantal slaapuren van studenten afwijkt van 8 uur.

Welke toets is passend?

A. t-toets voor één steekproef, want één gemiddelde wordt met een vaste waarde vergeleken.
B. t-toets voor twee onafhankelijke steekproeven, want de steekproef en de richtlijn zijn twee groepen.
C. Chikwadraattoets, want het aantal uren is een telling van hele uren.
D. Chikwadraattoets, want de studenten worden ingedeeld in voldoende en onvoldoende slaap.

### Vraag 10 (2 pt)

Een onderzoeker vraagt 120 eerstejaarsstudenten of ze een bijbaan hebben (ja of nee) en of ze overwegen te stoppen met de opleiding (ja of nee). De onderzoeksvraag is of een bijbaan samenhangt met het overwegen te stoppen.

Welke toets is passend?

A. t-toets voor één steekproef, want er is één groep van 120 studenten.
B. Chikwadraattoets, want beide variabelen zijn nominaal.
C. t-toets voor twee onafhankelijke steekproeven, want er zijn twee groepen (met en zonder bijbaan).
D. t-toets voor twee onafhankelijke steekproeven, want ja en nee zijn als 1 en 0 te coderen.

### Vraag 11 (2 pt)

Een psycholoog vergelijkt de gemiddelde score (0 tot 50 punten) op een geheugentest van 20 studenten die 's ochtends testten met 20 andere studenten die 's middags testten.

Welke toets is passend?

A. t-toets voor één steekproef, want de score is een intervalvariabele van alle 40 studenten samen.
B. Chikwadraattoets, want het testmoment (ochtend of middag) is een nominale variabele.
C. t-toets voor twee onafhankelijke steekproeven, want twee groepen worden op een intervalvariabele vergeleken.
D. Chikwadraattoets, want de score is een telling van het aantal goede antwoorden.

### Vraag 12 (2 pt)

Voor welke gegevens is de t-toets voor twee onafhankelijke steekproeven bedoeld?

A. Twee nominale variabelen.
B. Eén groep en een interval- of ratiovariabele.
C. Twee groepen en een nominale variabele.
D. Twee groepen en een interval- of ratiovariabele.

## Antwoordmodel

### Rij R1 — toepassen (vraag 1–2)

#### Vraag 1

De waarde t* = 2,064 komt uit de leerstof (95%, n = 25).

- a. (3 pt)

### Stage: blueprint

## Koppeling met de leeruitkomsten

- **EWS-score en actie** ("berekent een EWS-score bij een gegeven cliëntsituatie en noemt de actie die bij die score hoort volgens het afdelingsprotocol"): Toepassen. De student gebruikt de scoretabel op een nieuwe casus. Een lager niveau (Onthouden) toets ik alleen als voorwaarde: het kunnen noemen van de protocolactie bij een gegeven score.
- **Vitale functies meten en afwijkingen uitleggen**: niet opgenomen, zie "Niet opgenomen".

## Toetsmatrijs

| Rij | Leeruitkomst | Denkniveau | Vraagvorm | Aantal vragen | Punten per vraag | Punten |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R1 | EWS-score berekenen en actie noemen in een nieuwe casus | Toepassen | Open | 6 | 3 | 18 |
| R2 | Protocolactie noemen bij een gegeven score (voorwaarde) | Onthouden | Open | 2 | 1 | 2 |
| Totaal | | | | 8 | | 20 |

Toelichting voor stap 2:
- **R1:** elke vraag gaat over een nieuwe cliëntsituatie met een eigen set meetwaarden (ademhaling, saturatie, systolische bloeddruk, pols, temperatuur) die niet letterlijk in de leerstof staat. De student berekent de score per parameter, telt op en noemt de bijbehorende actie. Spreid de totaalscores over de vier protocolcategorieën (0–2, 3–4, 5–6, 7 of hoger).
- **R2:** de score is gegeven, de student noemt de actie volgens het protocol.

## Verdeling en punten

- Alle punten horen bij één opgenomen leeruitkomst: EWS-score en actie, 20 punten (100%). Binnen die leeruitkomst gaat 18 punten (90%) naar Toepassen en 2 punten (10%) naar de voorwaarde Onthouden.
- **Voorstel:** de punten per vraag (3 en 1) en het totaal van 20 punten. De docent gaf geen punten, dus dit is een voorstel. Toepassen krijgt het meeste gewicht, omdat de leeruitkomst om berekenen vraagt.
- **Voorstel:** alle 8 vragen vallen onder de ene opgenomen leeruitkomst, omdat de andere niet schriftelijk te toetsen is.
- Toetsduur, weging en cesuur zijn niet opgegeven. Ik doe daar geen voorstel voor en vul ze niet in.

## Niet opgenomen

**Leeruitkomst 1: "De student meet de vitale functies (pols, bloeddruk, ademhaling, temperatuur, saturatie) en legt uit welke waarden afwijken van de normaalwaarden."**

- **Waarom niet:** "meet" is een handeling die de student moet uitvoeren. Een schriftelijke toets kan dat niet beoordelen. Het tweede deel, uitleggen welke waarden afwijken, is wel schriftelijk te toetsen, maar de leeruitkomst als geheel niet.
- **Andere toetsvorm:** een praktijktoets met observatie, bijvoorbeeld een vaardigheidstoets in het skillslab of een beoordeling in de praktijk met een beoordelingsformulier.
- **Voorstel voor een herschreven leeruitkomst (schriftelijk toetsbaar, niveau Begrijpen, open vragen):** "De student legt uit welke waarden van pols, bloeddruk, ademhaling, temperatuur en saturatie in een gegeven cliëntsituatie afwijken van de normaalwaarden."
- **Verzoek:** pas de leeruitkomst aan in het formulier als u dit deel schriftelijk wilt toetsen. Ik pas de matrijs dan aan, met minstens twee vragen voor deze leeruitkomst.

- **Telt de matrijs op?** Ja: 6 + 2 = 8 vragen en 18 + 2 = 20 punten.
- **Toetst elke leeruitkomst op het denkniveau van het werkwoord?** Ja: 6 van de 8 vragen toetsen Toepassen ("berekent") in een nieuwe casus. De 2 vragen op Onthouden zijn de voorwaarde (de protocolactie kennen).
- **Heeft elke opgenomen leeruitkomst minstens twee vragen?** Ja: de enige opgenomen leeruitkomst heeft 8 vragen.
- **Past elke vraagvorm bij het denkniveau?** Ja: de docent vroeg alleen open vragen, en die passen bij zowel Toepassen met een casus als Onthouden.

## Koppeling met de leeruitkomsten

- **EWS-score en actie** ("berekent een EWS-score bij een gegeven cliëntsituatie en noemt de actie die bij die score hoort volgens het afdelingsprotocol"): Toepassen. De student gebruikt de scoretabel op een nieuwe casus. Een lager niveau (Onthouden) toets ik alleen als voorwaarde: het kunnen noemen van de protocolactie bij een gegeven score.
- **Vitale functies meten en afwijkingen uitleggen**: niet opgenomen, zie "Niet opgenomen".

## Toetsmatrijs

| Rij | Leeruitkomst | Denkniveau | Vraagvorm | Aantal vragen | Punten per vraag | Punten |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R1 | EWS-score berekenen en actie noemen in een nieuwe casus | Toepassen | Open | 6 | 3 | 18 |
| R2 | Protocolactie noemen bij een gegeven score (voorwaarde) | Onthouden | Open | 2 | 1 | 2 |
| Totaal | | | | 8 | | 20 |

Toelichting voor stap 2:
- **R1:** elke vraag gaat over een nieuwe cliëntsituatie met een eigen set meetwaarden (ademhaling, saturatie, systolische bloeddruk, pols, temperatuur) die niet letterlijk in de leerstof staat. De student berekent de score per parameter, telt op en noemt de bijbehorende actie. Spreid de totaalscores over de vier protocolcategorieën (0–2, 3–4, 5–6, 7 of hoger).
- **R2:** de score is gegeven, de student noemt de actie volgens het protocol.

## Verdeling en punten

- **Andere toetsvorm:** een praktijktoets met observatie, bijvoorbeeld een vaardigheidstoets in het skillslab of een beoordeling in de praktijk met een beoordelingsformulier.
- **Voorstel voor een herschreven leeruitkomst (schriftelijk toetsbaar, niveau Begrijpen, open vragen):** "De student legt uit welke waarden van pols, bloeddruk, ademhaling, temperatuur en saturatie in een gegeven cliëntsituatie afwijken van de normaalwaarden."
- **Verzoek:** pas de leeruitkomst aan in het formulier als u dit deel schriftelijk wilt toetsen. Ik pas de matrijs dan aan, met minstens twee vragen voor deze leeruitkomst.

- **Toetst elke leeruitkomst op het denkniveau van het werkwoord?** Ja: 6 van de 8 vragen toetsen Toepassen ("berekent") in een nieuwe casus. De 2 vragen op Onthouden zijn de voorwaarde (de protocolactie kennen).
- **Heeft elke opgenomen leeruitkomst minstens twee vragen?** Ja: de enige opgenomen leeruitkomst heeft 8 vragen.

### Stage: blueprint

## Link to the learning outcomes

- **Outcome 1: The student identifies threats to internal and external validity in a described study.** The verb "identify" is applied here to a described case. The student classifies what happens in the case under a known threat category, so the cognitive level is **Understand** (classify). The prerequisite is knowing the definitions of the threats (Remember). That is tested only indirectly, through the case questions, and no separate Remember questions are included.
- **Outcome 2: The student evaluates whether a described research design can answer a given causal research question.** The verb "evaluate" asks for a judgement against criteria (can the design support a causal claim?). The cognitive level is **Evaluate**, tested with a case. The prerequisite is recognising the threats that each design cannot rule out (Outcome 1). It is not tested separately.

## Test blueprint

### Question 1 (1 pt)
A school introduces a new reading programme for all Grade 3 pupils. Reading scores are measured in September, before the programme, and again in January. There is no comparison group. The scores rise on average. In November, a free public library opened next to the school, and many pupils started borrowing books.

Which threat to internal validity is most clearly present?

A. Maturation (natural change over time)
B. Selection (non-equivalent groups)
C. History (an event during the study)
D. Testing (effect of a pretest)

### Question 2 (1 pt)
A school gives extra tutoring to the 15 pupils with the lowest scores on a maths test. Eight weeks later, these pupils take the same test again. Their average score is higher. No other pupils are tested again. The school concludes that the tutoring worked.

Which threat to internal validity, linked to how the pupils were chosen, may explain part of the rise?

A. Regression to the mean (extreme groups selected)
B. Selection (non-equivalent groups)
C. Attrition (differential drop-out)
D. Instrumentation (change in measurement)

### Question 3 (1 pt)
A researcher randomly assigns 200 students to a mentoring programme (100 students) or a control group (100 students). After one year, 30 programme students and 5 control students have stopped taking part in the study. Most of the 30 said that the mentoring asked too much of them. Well-being is measured only in the students who remain. The programme group scores higher. The researcher concludes that mentoring improves well-being.

Which threat to internal validity weakens this conclusion most?

A. Selection (non-equivalent groups)
B. History (an event during the study)
C. Maturation (natural change over time)
D. Attrition (differential drop-out)

### Question 4 (1 pt)
A researcher recruits volunteers at one private secondary school in a wealthy neighbourhood. The volunteers are randomly assigned to a concentration programme or to a control group. The programme is given during regular lessons in the pupils' own classrooms. All pupils complete the study, and the programme group concentrates better. The researcher concludes that the programme improves concentration in all secondary-school pupils in the country.

Which threat to validity most limits this conclusion?

A. Selection (non-equivalent groups)
B. Unrepresentative sample
C. Artificial setting
D. Attrition (differential drop-out)

### Question 5 (1 pt)
A teacher training college evaluates a writing course with 40 students. At the start, an assessor scores each student's essay with a detailed rubric on a scale of 1 to 10. At the end, a different assessor scores the new essays with a shorter and more lenient scale. The scores rise on average.

Which threat to internal validity is most clearly present?

A. Testing (effect of a pretest)
B. Maturation (natural change over time)
C. Instrumentation (change in measurement)
D. Regression to the mean (extreme groups selected)

### Question 6 (1 pt)
An educational researcher wants to know whether a new homework policy raises pupils' motivation. One class fills in a motivation questionnaire at the start of the semester and again at the end, after the policy has been in place. The scores are higher at the end. No other class is measured.

Which judgement of this design is correct?

A. The design supports a causal claim, because measuring the same pupils twice rules out differences between groups.
B. The design does not support a causal claim, because history, maturation and regression to the mean are not ruled out.
C. The design supports a causal claim, because the rise came after the policy was introduced.
D. The design does not support a causal claim, because the direction of the effect cannot be established.

### Question 7 (1 pt)
A researcher asks: does a tutoring programme raise pass rates? In total, 120 students who signed up for tutoring are randomly assigned to tutoring or to a waiting list. At the end of the term, the pass rates of the two groups are compared. All students stay in the study.

Which judgement of this design is correct?

A. The design does not support a causal claim, because students who sign up differ from other students, so the groups are non-equivalent.
B. The design does not support a causal claim, because no pretest was taken.
C. The design supports a causal claim only if the 120 students are representative of all students.
D. The design supports a causal claim for these students, because random assignment controls selection.

### Question 8 (1 pt)
A researcher asks: does a mentoring programme reduce first-year drop-out? School A offers the programme to all first-year students. School B does not. The schools differ in size and student intake. Drop-out is counted only once, at the end of the year.

Which change would most strengthen the ability of this design to answer the causal question?

A. Measure the students' drop-out risk at both schools before the programme starts, and take differences at the start into account.
B. Include more first-year students from both schools in the end-of-year count of drop-out.
C. Count drop-out at School A again at the end of the following year.
D. Add a third school that offers the programme, again with drop-out counted only at the end of the year.

### Question 9 (1 pt)
A researcher asks: does using a study app raise students' grades? A questionnaire is given once to 300 students. It asks for weekly hours of app use and for the average grade. The researcher finds a strong positive correlation between the two.

Which judgement of this design is correct?

A. The design supports the causal claim, because a strong correlation in 300 students is unlikely to be due to chance.
B. The design does not support the causal claim, because the direction of the effect cannot be established.
C. The design does not support the causal claim, because history and maturation are not ruled out in one survey.
D. The design supports the causal claim for these students, but not for other students.

### Question 10 (1 pt)
A policy advisor wants to answer this question: does a new teacher training raise pupils' reading scores?

Which design can best answer this question?

A. Ask teachers how many hours of training they had and relate this to their pupils' reading scores.
B. Compare pupils of teachers who chose the training with pupils of teachers who did not, at the end of the year.
C. Randomly assign teachers to the training or to a waiting list and compare their pupils' reading scores afterwards.
D. Measure the reading scores of the trained teachers' pupils before and after the training.

## Answer model

### Row R1 — Understand (questions 1–5)

#### Question 1
**Correct answer:** C. The library that opened during the study is an outside event that may have raised reading scores, which is history.
**A:** Maturation is natural change in the pupils themselves over time. The case describes a specific outside event, so the student has mixed up an outside event with natural development.
**B:** Selection needs two groups that differ from the start. The case has only one group, so the student has mixed up the one-group case with a group comparison.
**D:** Testing is the effect of taking the pretest itself. Nothing in the case suggests that the September test raised the January scores, so the student has chosen the generic pre–post threat.

#### Question 2
**Correct answer:** A. Pupils were chosen because of their extreme (low) scores, so on retest their scores tend to move towards the average without any effect of the tutoring.
**B:** Selection concerns non-equivalent groups. The case has no comparison group, so the student has confused "selected pupils" with "selection threat".
**C:** Attrition is differential drop-out. The case does not mention that any pupil left.
**D:** Instrumentation is a change in measurement. The same test is used both times, so the measurement did not change.

#### Question 3
**Correct answer:** D. Far more programme students than control students left, and mostly those who found the programme too demanding. The remaining programme group is therefore no longer comparable to the control group, which is differential drop-out.
**A:** Selection is ruled out at the start because of random assignment. A student who sees "groups differ at the end" and thinks of selection has overlooked that the difference arose through drop-out.
**B:** History is an outside event during the study. No such event is described.
**C:** Maturation is natural change over time. It would affect both groups equally and does not explain the unequal drop-out.

#### Question 4
**Correct answer:** B. The volunteers come from one private school in a wealthy neighbourhood, so they do not represent all secondary-school pupils, and the conclusion is about all pupils in the country (external validity).
**A:** Random assignment makes the groups equivalent, so selection is not the problem. The student has mixed up internal validity (comparability of groups) with external validity (generalisation).
**C:** The programme is given in regular lessons in the pupils' own classrooms, so the setting is not artificial.
**D:** All pupils complete the study, so there is no drop-out.

#### Question 5
**Correct answer:** C. The essays are scored with a different, more lenient scale by a different assessor, so the measurement changed between pretest and posttest (instrumentation).
**A:** Testing is the effect of having taken a pretest. The case describes a change in the scoring, not an effect of earlier practice.
**B:** Maturation is natural change in the students over time. The case gives a more direct explanation, the changed scoring, and a student who chooses this uses a generic explanation for any pre–post rise.
**D:** Regression to the mean needs a group selected for extreme scores. The 40 students are not selected on extreme scores.

### Row R2 — Evaluate (questions 6–10)

#### Question 6
**Correct answer:** B. A one-group pretest–posttest design has no comparison group, so history, maturation and regression to the mean cannot be ruled out.
**A:** With one group there is no group comparison, so this feature does not rule out the three threats that matter here. The student has mixed up "same pupils" with "equivalent groups".
**C:** A rise after the policy shows only that the scores changed after it. The change may equally be caused by history or maturation, so the student has mistaken time order for causation.
**D:** The direction of the effect is a problem of correlational designs. Here the measurements are taken before and after, so the order in time is clear. The student has mixed up two designs.

#### Question 7
**Correct answer:** D. Random assignment makes the two groups equivalent and so controls selection, which supports a causal claim for these students.
**A:** Random assignment within the volunteers makes the groups equivalent, even though volunteers differ from other students. The student has mixed up the effect of signing up on the groups' comparability with its effect on generalisation.
**B:** A randomised controlled trial does not need a pretest to control selection. The student has transferred the pretest requirement of the non-equivalent-groups quasi-experiment.
**C:** Representativeness concerns external validity, not whether the causal claim holds for the students studied. The student has mixed up internal and external validity.

#### Question 8
**Correct answer:** A. A quasi-experiment with non-equivalent groups needs a pretest and control for selection, and this option adds both.
**B:** More students do not remove differences between the schools, so selection stays uncontrolled. The student thinks that a larger sample solves a design problem.
**C:** A second count at School A alone gives no information about the differences between the schools. It also moves towards a one-group design.
**D:** A third school with the programme and no pretest adds another uncontrolled comparison and does not control selection.

#### Question 9
**Correct answer:** B. A correlational design cannot establish the direction of an effect. High grades may lead to more app use, as well as the reverse.
**A:** The strength of a correlation and the sample size do not tell us the direction of the effect. The student confuses statistical strength with causal evidence.
**C:** History and maturation are threats in designs that measure change over time. A single survey measures no change, so the reason given is wrong. The student has mixed up the weakness of correlational designs with that of pre–post designs.
**D:** The design cannot support a causal claim for any students, so the limit is not about generalising to other students. The student has mixed up internal and external validity.

#### Question 10
**Correct answer:** C. A randomised controlled trial supports causal claims best, because random assignment controls selection.
**A:** A correlational design cannot establish the direction of an effect, so it is the weakest of the four designs for a causal question.
**B:** This comparison has non-equivalent groups, with teachers who chose the training. It has neither a pretest nor control for selection, so differences may already have existed.
**D:** A one-group pretest–posttest design cannot rule out history, maturation and regression, so it is weaker than random assignment.

- **Does every multiple-choice question have exactly one correct answer?** Yes, because in each case the material decides the answer and every distractor is wrong according to it.

- **Are all distractors plausible?** Yes, because each one is a real confusion, such as mixing internal with external validity, one design with another, or a statistical argument with a causal one.

- **Does everything follow from the material?** Yes, because all threats, designs and judgements come from the material, and only the cases are invented.
- **Does any question give away the answer to another?** No, because each question has its own case and none needs the answer to another.

#### Question 10
**Correct answer:** C. A randomised controlled trial supports causal claims best, because random assignment controls selection.
**A:** A correlational design cannot establish the direction of an effect, so it is the weakest of the four designs for a causal question.
**B:** This comparison has non-equivalent groups, with teachers who chose the training. It has neither a pretest nor control for selection, so differences may already have existed.
**D:** A one-group pretest–posttest design cannot rule out history, maturation and regression, so it is weaker than random assignment.

### Stage: blueprint

## Link to the learning outcomes

- **Outcome 1: The student identifies threats to internal and external validity in a described study.** Cognitive level: Apply. The student uses the known threat categories on a new, described study. This is not a Remember question, because the case is not an example from the material. No lower-level prerequisite question is included.
- **Outcome 2: The student evaluates whether a described research design can answer a given causal research question.** Cognitive level: Evaluate. The student judges the design against criteria (internal validity, control of selection, direction of effect) and justifies a conclusion about the causal question. Multiple choice can test this with a new case.

## Test blueprint

| Row | Learning outcome | Cognitive level | Question type | Number of questions | Points per question | Points |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R1 | Identify threats to internal and external validity in a described study | Apply | Multiple choice | 4 | 1 | 4 |
| R2 | Evaluate whether a research design can answer a causal research question | Evaluate | Multiple choice | 6 | 1 | 6 |
| Total | | | | 10 | | 10 |

## Distribution and points

- **Total:** 10 questions at 1 point each gives 10 points. This comes from the teacher.
- **Outcome 1 (R1):** 4 points, 40% of the total. Proposal.
- **Outcome 2 (R2):** 6 points, 60% of the total. Proposal. The teacher gave no weighting. I weighted outcome 2 more heavily because it asks for a higher cognitive process and covers four designs, each needing its own judgement.
- **Test duration:** 45 minutes, from the teacher. Time estimate (Proposal), based on case-based multiple choice with a short case text:
  - R1: 4 questions × about 2.5 minutes = about 10 minutes.
  - R2: 6 questions × about 3.5 minutes = about 21 minutes.
  - Total: about 31 minutes, which leaves about 14 minutes for reading, checking and a margin. The test fits in 45 minutes.
- **Pass mark:** the teacher gave none, so none is set here.
- **Coverage within the rows (Proposal for step 2):** R1 should cover both internal threats (selection, history, maturation, testing, instrumentation, regression to the mean, attrition) and external threats (unrepresentative sample, artificial setting). R2 should cover the four designs in the material: randomised controlled trial, quasi-experiment with non-equivalent groups, one-group pretest–posttest, and correlational design. Every question needs a new case that does not appear literally in the material.

## Self-check

- **Does the blueprint add up?** Yes. The questions are 4 + 6 = 10, and the points are 4 + 6 = 10, which matches the teacher's total of 10 points at 1 point per question.
- **Does every outcome get tested at the level of its verb?** Yes. R1 tests Apply and R2 tests Evaluate, and neither goes beyond what its verb asks.
- **Does every outcome included have at least two questions?** Yes. Outcome 1 has 4 questions and outcome 2 has 6.
- **Does every question type fit its cognitive level?** Yes. Multiple choice can test Apply with a case, and Evaluate with a case, and the teacher allows only multiple choice.

This is a draft. The teacher decides on the test.

### Stage: items

## Questions

### Question 1 (1 pt)
A school tests a new writing course. In September, Ms Jansen grades all students' essays. In December, after the course, Mr Bakker grades the essays because Ms Jansen is ill. He uses looser grading criteria. The students score higher in December.

Which threat to internal validity is introduced by the way the essays were graded?

A. Testing
B. Instrumentation
C. Maturation
D. History

### Question 2 (1 pt)
A school gives all 200 first-year students a maths test in October. The 20 students with the lowest scores join extra tutoring. In January, these 20 students take a different maths test of equal difficulty. Their average score is higher than in October.

Which threat to internal validity follows directly from how these students were selected?

A. Maturation
B. Testing
C. Regression to the mean
D. History

### Question 3 (1 pt)
A company randomly assigns 100 employees to a stress-reduction course (50) or a waiting list (50). After six months, 20 employees in the course group have left the study, mostly people who found the course too demanding because of their high workload. Only 2 employees in the waiting-list group have left. The remaining course participants report lower stress than the waiting-list group.

Which threat to internal validity does this describe?

A. Attrition
B. Selection
C. Instrumentation
D. History

### Question 4 (1 pt)
Researchers test a feedback app that is meant for regular classrooms. They randomly select 400 students from schools across the country and randomly assign them to the app or to a control condition. Each student works alone in a quiet university lab room, with a researcher watching. The app group scores higher. The researchers conclude that the app also works in regular classrooms.

Which threat to external validity is the most important problem for this conclusion?

A. Unrepresentative sample
B. Selection
C. Artificial setting
D. Instrumentation

### Question 5 (1 pt)
A municipality gives the pupils of one primary school a free breakfast for a year. Absence rates in the year before (pretest) and the year after (posttest) are compared. The absence rate fell. A policy adviser wants to know whether the free breakfast caused the fall.

Which evaluation of this design is correct?

A. It can answer the question, because the same pupils are measured twice, so other explanations are ruled out.
B. It can answer the question, because a fall after the breakfast started shows the breakfast caused it.
C. It cannot answer the question, because other events or natural change during the year could also explain the fall.
D. It cannot answer the question, because pupils were not randomly assigned, so selection explains the fall.

### Question 6 (1 pt)
A survey among 300 students at one college measures weekly use of a study-planning app and each student's grade average. Students who use the app more have higher grades. A policy adviser concludes: "The app raises grades, so we should require its use."

Which evaluation of this conclusion is correct?

A. It is justified, because a clear correlation shows that the app causes higher grades.
B. It is not justified, because the direction is unknown: students with high grades may use the app more.
C. It is not justified, because a correlational design cannot show any relationship between two variables.
D. It is not justified, because the survey has no pretest, so regression to the mean explains the correlation.

### Question 7 (1 pt)
A teacher wants to know whether a new peer-tutoring programme improves reading scores. She gives the programme to her own class (class 1). She does not give it to a parallel class (class 2), which she picked because it looked similar. At the end of the term, only a reading test is taken. Class 1 scores higher than class 2.

Can this design answer the causal question?

A. No, because differences between the classes before the programme could explain the posttest difference.
B. Yes, because comparing with a control class rules out all threats to internal validity.
C. Yes, because the teacher knows the classes well and so picked comparable ones.
D. No, because with only one outcome measure the direction of the effect stays unclear.

### Question 8 (1 pt)
A municipality will offer a homework-support programme in two of its neighbourhoods. Random assignment of residents is not possible. A policy adviser must choose a design to find out whether the programme improves pupils' grades.

Which design is best able to answer this causal question?

A. Measure grades before and after the programme in the two neighbourhoods, without a comparison group.
B. Survey pupils in all neighbourhoods on programme use and grades, then correlate the two.
C. Compare grades after the programme in the two neighbourhoods with grades in two other neighbourhoods.
D. Measure grades before and after in the two neighbourhoods and in two other neighbourhoods, and control for pretest differences.

### Question 9 (1 pt)
Researchers randomly assign 200 pupils from several schools to a tutoring programme (100 pupils) or a control group (100 pupils). Both groups take the same test before and after the programme. No pupil dropped out. The tutoring group improves more. A reviewer asks whether this design can support the claim that tutoring caused the extra improvement for these pupils.

Which evaluation is correct?

A. No, because an experiment shows only that two variables are related, not which came first.
B. Yes, because random assignment controls selection, so the groups differ only by chance.
C. No, because causal claims need groups matched on pupil characteristics, which random assignment does not do.
D. No, because causal claims need a study in a natural setting, and an experiment does not provide one.

### Question 10 (1 pt)
Researchers randomly assign 120 volunteers from one private school to a tutoring programme or to a control group. The tutoring group scores higher. The authors conclude: "Tutoring improves results for all secondary-school pupils."

Which evaluation of this conclusion is correct?

A. It is justified, because random assignment makes the results generalise to all pupils.
B. It is not justified, because the use of volunteers means selection threatens internal validity.
C. The effect for these pupils is supported, but generalising to all pupils is not, because the sample is unrepresentative.
D. It is not justified, because a randomised design cannot show whether tutoring or something else caused the difference.

## Answer model

### Row R1 — Apply (questions 1–4)

#### Question 1
**Correct answer:** B. The change of grader and criteria between pretest and posttest is a change in measurement, which is instrumentation.
**A:** Wrong. Testing is the effect of having taken a pretest. The case is about a different grader, not about practice. It catches students who see any pretest–posttest design as a testing problem.
**C:** Wrong. Maturation is natural change in the students over time. The question asks about a threat introduced by the grading. It catches students who name the most familiar threat for a before–after design.
**D:** Wrong. History is an outside event during the study. The case describes no such event, only a change in how essays were graded. It catches students who mix up "something changed" with "an event happened".

#### Question 2
**Correct answer:** C. The students were selected because they scored extremely low, so their scores are expected to move towards the average on a retest even without tutoring.
**A:** Wrong. Maturation is natural development over time. The question asks which threat follows from the way the students were selected, and that is extreme scores. It catches students who think any improvement without a control group is maturation.
**B:** Wrong. A different test of equal difficulty was used, so practice from the pretest is not the issue. It catches students who see "tested twice" and name testing.
**D:** Wrong. The case names no outside event. It catches students who treat "time passed between two measurements" as history.

#### Question 3
**Correct answer:** A. Many more people left the course group than the waiting-list group, and the leavers were those with high workload. This is differential drop-out, which is attrition.
**B:** Wrong. Selection is non-equivalent groups at the start. Here the groups were randomly assigned, so the problem arose later through drop-out. It catches students who confuse unequal groups at the end with unequal groups at the start.
**C:** Wrong. Nothing in the case says the way stress was measured changed. It catches students who think any biased outcome is a measurement problem.
**D:** Wrong. The case names no outside event during the six months. It catches students who pick a threat by its general sound instead of by the case.

#### Question 4
**Correct answer:** C. Working alone in a lab with a researcher watching differs from a regular classroom, so this is an artificial setting.
**A:** Wrong. The students were randomly selected from schools across the country, so the sample is not the problem. It catches students who assume every generalisation problem is a sample problem.
**B:** Wrong. Selection is an internal validity threat, and random assignment controls it here. The question asks about external validity. It catches students who mix up internal and external threats.
**D:** Wrong. Instrumentation is an internal validity threat and nothing in the case suggests a change in measurement. It catches the same mix-up of internal and external threats.

### Row R2 — Evaluate (questions 5–10)

#### Question 5
**Correct answer:** C. A one-group pretest–posttest design cannot rule out history, maturation and regression, so other events or natural change could explain the fall.
**A:** Wrong. Measuring the same pupils twice does not rule out other explanations. It catches students who think a pretest controls everything.
**B:** Wrong. A change after an intervention does not prove the intervention caused it; this is the "after, so because" error. History and maturation remain possible.
**D:** Wrong. With one group there are no two groups to be non-equivalent, so selection is not the problem. The real problems are history, maturation and regression. It catches students who equate "no random assignment" with "selection explains the result".

#### Question 6
**Correct answer:** B. A correlational design cannot establish the direction of an effect, so higher grades could lead to more app use.
**A:** Wrong. A correlation alone does not show cause or direction. It catches the common mistake of reading a clear correlation as proof of cause.
**C:** Wrong. A correlational design can show that two variables are related. It cannot show direction. It catches students who overstate the limit of correlational research.
**D:** Wrong. Regression to the mean concerns the selection of extreme groups and a later measurement. It does not explain a correlation in a single survey. It catches students who mix up threat concepts.

#### Question 7
**Correct answer:** A. The class was chosen by the teacher and there is no pretest, so differences that existed before the programme (selection) could explain the posttest difference.
**B:** Wrong. A comparison class does not rule out all threats. Without random assignment or a pretest, selection remains. It catches students who think any control group makes a design causal.
**C:** Wrong. The teacher's judgement that the classes look similar is not a control for selection. A pretest and control for selection are needed. It catches students who trust informal matching.
**D:** Wrong. The number of outcome measures is not the issue, and the problem is not the direction of the effect. That limit belongs to correlational designs. It catches students who mix up the limits of different designs.

#### Question 8
**Correct answer:** D. A quasi-experiment with non-equivalent groups needs a pretest and control for selection, and option D has both plus a comparison group.
**A:** Wrong. A one-group pretest–posttest design cannot rule out history, maturation and regression. It catches students who think a pretest alone is enough.
**B:** Wrong. A correlational design cannot establish the direction of an effect. It catches students who think a large survey can answer a causal question.
**C:** Wrong. A comparison group without a pretest cannot show whether the neighbourhoods already differed (selection). It catches students who think a comparison group alone is enough.

#### Question 9
**Correct answer:** B. Random assignment controls selection, so the groups differ only by chance. With no drop-out and the same measurement, the design supports the causal claim for these pupils.
**A:** Wrong. An experiment manipulates the intervention before the outcome is measured, so the direction is known. The direction problem belongs to correlational designs. It catches students who mix up experiments and correlational designs.
**C:** Wrong. Random assignment, not matching, is what controls selection. It catches students who think only deliberate matching makes groups comparable.
**D:** Wrong. A randomised trial supports causal claims best. Setting is a question of external validity and does not remove the causal claim for these pupils. It catches students who mix up internal and external validity.

#### Question 10
**Correct answer:** C. Random assignment supports the causal claim within the sample, but a sample from one private school is unrepresentative, so generalising to all pupils is not supported.
**A:** Wrong. Random assignment controls selection, which is about internal validity. It does not make a sample representative. It catches students who think random assignment secures external validity.
**B:** Wrong. Random assignment among the volunteers still creates equivalent groups. Volunteering limits generalisation, not the comparison between the two groups. It catches students who mix up selection into the study with selection into groups.
**D:** Wrong. A randomised design supports causal claims best, because random assignment controls selection. It catches students who doubt experiments for the wrong reason.

## Check against the blueprint

| Row | Planned | Written | Questions |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R1 | 4 | 4 | 1, 2, 3, 4 |
| R2 | 6 | 6 | 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 |
| Total | 10 questions, 10 points | 10 questions, 10 points | 1–10 |

Correct answers by position: A = 2 (questions 3, 7), B = 3 (questions 1, 6, 9), C = 3 (questions 4, 5, 10), D = 2 (questions 2, 8).

I saw no error in the blueprint. Notes on coverage:
- R1 uses instrumentation, regression to the mean, attrition and artificial setting as the correct answers.
- The other threats from the material (selection, history, maturation, testing, unrepresentative sample) appear as distractors or in R2.
- R2 covers the randomised controlled trial twice (9, 10), the quasi-experiment twice (7, 8), the one-group pretest–posttest once (5) and the correlational design once (6).
- Question 10 also touches external validity, which fits the evaluation of what an RCT does and does not support.

## Self-check

- **Does every multiple-choice question have exactly one correct answer?** Yes, each stem names a specific threat or design limit that the material settles, and each distractor is wrong under the material.
- **Is there no clue to the correct answer anywhere?** Yes, I balanced option lengths and form and spread the correct answers over A to D. Option C in question 10 is slightly longer because it has two parts, and the same-length options lessen that effect.
- **Are all distractors plausible?** Yes, each distractor is a real misconception, such as confusing internal and external validity, or reading a correlation as cause.
- **Does every question test the cognitive level of its row?** Yes. Questions 1–4 apply threat categories to new cases. Questions 5–10 judge whether a design can answer a causal question.
- **Does everything follow from the material?** Yes, all cases are new and fictitious and given in full, and all judgements follow from the threats and designs in the material.
- **Does any question give away the answer to another?** No, each case is self-contained and no question needs another's answer.

This is a draft. The teacher decides on the test.

C. Yes, because the teacher knows the classes well and so picked comparable ones.
D. No, because with only one outcome measure the direction of the effect stays unclear.

### Question 8 (1 pt)
A municipality will offer a homework-support programme in two of its neighbourhoods. Random assignment of residents is not possible. A policy adviser must choose a design to find out whether the programme improves pupils' grades.

Which design is best able to answer this causal question?

A. Measure grades before and after the programme in the two neighbourhoods, without a comparison group.
B. Survey pupils in all neighbourhoods on programme use and grades, then correlate the two.
C. Compare grades after the programme in the two neighbourhoods with grades in two other neighbourhoods.
D. Measure grades before and after in the two neighbourhoods and in two other neighbourhoods, and control for pretest differences.

### Question 9 (1 pt)
Researchers randomly assign 200 pupils from several schools to a tutoring programme (100 pupils) or a control group (100 pupils). Both groups take the same test before and after the programme. No pupil dropped out. The tutoring group improves more. A reviewer asks whether this design can support the claim that tutoring caused the extra improvement for these pupils.

Which evaluation is correct?

A. No, because an experiment shows only that two variables are related, not which came first.
B. Yes, because random assignment controls selection, so the groups differ only by chance.
C. No, because causal claims need groups matched on pupil characteristics, which random assignment does not do.
D. No, because causal claims need a study in a natural setting, and an experiment does not provide one.

### Question 10 (1 pt)
Researchers randomly assign 120 volunteers from one private school to a tutoring programme or to a control group. The tutoring group scores higher. The authors conclude: "Tutoring improves results for all secondary-school pupils."

Which evaluation of this conclusion is correct?

A. It is justified, because random assignment makes the results generalise to all pupils.
B. It is not justified, because the use of volunteers means selection threatens internal validity.
C. The effect for these pupils is supported, but generalising to all pupils is not, because the sample is unrepresentative.
D. It is not justified, because a randomised design cannot show whether tutoring or something else caused the difference.

## Answer model

### Row R1 — Apply (questions 1–4)

#### Question 1
**Correct answer:** B. The change of grader and criteria between pretest and posttest is a change in measurement, which is instrumentation.
**A:** Wrong. Testing is the effect of having taken a pretest. The case is about a different grader, not about practice. It catches students who see any pretest–posttest design as a testing problem.
**C:** Wrong. Maturation is natural change in the students over time. The question asks about a threat introduced by the grading. It catches students who name the most familiar threat for a before–after design.
**D:** Wrong. History is an outside event during the study. The case describes no such event, only a change in how essays were graded. It catches students who mix up "something changed" with "an event happened".

#### Question 2
**Correct answer:** C. The students were selected because they scored extremely low, so their scores are expected to move towards the average on a retest even without tutoring.
**A:** Wrong. Maturation is natural development over time. The question asks which threat follows from the way the students were selected, and that is extreme scores. It catches students who think any improvement without a control group is maturation.
**B:** Wrong. A different test of equal difficulty was used, so practice from the pretest is not the issue. It catches students who see "tested twice" and name testing.
**D:** Wrong. The case names no outside event. It catches students who treat "time passed between two measurements" as history.

#### Question 3
**Correct answer:** A. Many more people left the course group than the waiting-list group, and the leavers were those with high workload. This is differential drop-out, which is attrition.
**B:** Wrong. Selection is non-equivalent groups at the start. Here the groups were randomly assigned, so the problem arose later through drop-out. It catches students who confuse unequal groups at the end with unequal groups at the start.
**C:** Wrong. Nothing in the case says the way stress was measured changed. It catches students who think any biased outcome is a measurement problem.
**D:** Wrong. The case names no outside event during the six months. It catches students who pick a threat by its general sound instead of by the case.

#### Question 4
**Correct answer:** C. Working alone in a lab with a researcher watching differs from a regular classroom, so this is an artificial setting.
**A:** Wrong. The students were randomly selected from schools across the country, so the sample is not the problem. It catches students who assume every generalisation problem is a sample problem.
**B:** Wrong. Selection is an internal validity threat, and random assignment controls it here. The question asks about external validity. It catches students who mix up internal and external threats.
**D:** Wrong. Instrumentation is an internal validity threat and nothing in the case suggests a change in measurement. It catches the same mix-up of internal and external threats.

### Row R2 — Evaluate (questions 5–10)

#### Question 5
**Correct answer:** C. A one-group pretest–posttest design cannot rule out history, maturation and regression, so other events or natural change could explain the fall.
**A:** Wrong. Measuring the same pupils twice does not rule out other explanations. It catches students who think a pretest controls everything.
**B:** Wrong. A change after an intervention does not prove the intervention caused it; this is the "after, so because" error. History and maturation remain possible.
**D:** Wrong. With one group there are no two groups to be non-equivalent, so selection is not the problem. The real problems are history, maturation and regression. It catches students who equate "no random assignment" with "selection explains the result".

#### Question 6
**Correct answer:** B. A correlational design cannot establish the direction of an effect, so higher grades could lead to more app use.
**A:** Wrong. A correlation alone does not show cause or direction. It catches the common mistake of reading a clear correlation as proof of cause.
**C:** Wrong. A correlational design can show that two variables are related. It cannot show direction. It catches students who overstate the limit of correlational research.
**D:** Wrong. Regression to the mean concerns the selection of extreme groups and a later measurement. It does not explain a correlation in a single survey. It catches students who mix up threat concepts.

#### Question 7
**Correct answer:** A. The class was chosen by the teacher and there is no pretest, so differences that existed before the programme (selection) could explain the posttest difference.
**B:** Wrong. A comparison class does not rule out all threats. Without random assignment or a pretest, selection remains. It catches students who think any control group makes a design causal.
**C:** Wrong. The teacher's judgement that the classes look similar is not a control for selection. A pretest and control for selection are needed. It catches students who trust informal matching.
**D:** Wrong. The number of outcome measures is not the issue, and the problem is not the direction of the effect. That limit belongs to correlational designs. It catches students who mix up the limits of different designs.

#### Question 8
**Correct answer:** D. A quasi-experiment with non-equivalent groups needs a pretest and control for selection, and option D has both plus a comparison group.
**A:** Wrong. A one-group pretest–posttest design cannot rule out history, maturation and regression. It catches students who think a pretest alone is enough.
**B:** Wrong. A correlational design cannot establish the direction of an effect. It catches students who think a large survey can answer a causal question.
**C:** Wrong. A comparison group without a pretest cannot show whether the neighbourhoods already differed (selection). It catches students who think a comparison group alone is enough.

#### Question 9
**Correct answer:** B. Random assignment controls selection, so the groups differ only by chance. With no drop-out and the same measurement, the design supports the causal claim for these pupils.
**A:** Wrong. An experiment manipulates the intervention before the outcome is measured, so the direction is known. The direction problem belongs to correlational designs. It catches students who mix up experiments and correlational designs.
**C:** Wrong. Random assignment, not matching, is what controls selection. It catches students who think only deliberate matching makes groups comparable.
**D:** Wrong. A randomised trial supports causal claims best. Setting is a question of external validity and does not remove the causal claim for these pupils. It catches students who mix up internal and external validity.

#### Question 10
**Correct answer:** C. Random assignment supports the causal claim within the sample, but a sample from one private school is unrepresentative, so generalising to all pupils is not supported.
**A:** Wrong. Random assignment controls selection, which is about internal validity. It does not make a sample representative. It catches students who think random assignment secures external validity.
**B:** Wrong. Random assignment among the volunteers still creates equivalent groups. Volunteering limits generalisation, not the comparison between the two groups. It catches students who mix up selection into the study with selection into groups.
**D:** Wrong. A randomised design supports causal claims best, because random assignment controls selection. It catches students who doubt experiments for the wrong reason.

## Self-check

- **Does every multiple-choice question have exactly one correct answer?** Yes, each stem names a specific threat or design limit that the material settles, and each distractor is wrong under the material.
- **Is there no clue to the correct answer anywhere?** Yes, I balanced option lengths and form and spread the correct answers over A to D. Option C in question 10 is slightly longer because it has two parts, and the same-length options lessen that effect.

### Stage: blueprint

## Link to the learning outcomes

- **The student identifies threats to internal and external validity in a described study:** Understand (classifying a situation in a new case under the right threat). Every question uses a new case. No lower-level prerequisite questions are included.
- **The student evaluates whether a described research design can answer a given causal research question:** Evaluate (judging a design against the criterion of causal inference, using a new case).

## Test blueprint

| Row | Learning outcome | Cognitive level | Question type | Number of questions | Points per question | Points |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R1 | Identify threats to internal and external validity in a described study | Understand | Multiple choice | 4 | 1 | 4 |
| R2 | Evaluate whether a research design can answer a causal research question | Evaluate | Multiple choice | 6 | 1 | 6 |
| Total | | | | 10 | | 10 |

## Distribution and points

The teacher gave 10 questions, 10 points in total, one point per question and 45 minutes. The blueprint matches these figures. The teacher gave no weighting and no pass mark.

- **Identify threats (R1):** 4 points, 40% of the total. **Proposal.**
- **Evaluate design (R2):** 6 points, 60% of the total. **Proposal.**
- **Reason for the weighting (Proposal):** the evaluate outcome asks for the higher and more integrative judgement. It also draws on recognising threats, so it gets more weight.
- **Coverage within R1 (Proposal):** use at least one question on external validity, and spread the other questions over the internal threats in the material (selection, history, maturation, testing, instrumentation, regression to the mean, attrition).
- **Coverage within R2 (Proposal):** spread the questions over the four designs in the material (randomised controlled trial, quasi-experiment with non-equivalent groups, one-group pretest–posttest, correlational design).
- **Time estimate (Proposal):**
  - R1: 4 questions × about 3 minutes = about 12 minutes.
  - R2: 6 questions × about 4 minutes = about 24 minutes.
  - Total: about 36 minutes. This leaves about 9 minutes for reading and checking, so the test fits in 45 minutes.
- **Pass mark:** not given by the teacher, so none is set here.

## Self-check

- **Does the blueprint add up?** Yes. The questions are 4 + 6 = 10 and the points are 4 + 6 = 10.
- **Does every outcome get tested at the level of its verb?** Yes. R1 tests Understand (classifying threats in a case) and R2 tests Evaluate (judging a design in a case). Neither goes higher than its verb asks.
- **Does every outcome included have at least two questions?** Yes. R1 has 4 questions and R2 has 6.
- **Does every question type fit its cognitive level?** Yes. Multiple choice can measure Understand, and it can measure Evaluate when a case is used. Both rows must use cases that do not appear literally in the material.

### Stage: items

## Questions

### Question 1 (1 pt)
At a school, pupils who signed up for a reading programme are randomly assigned: 60 to the programme and 60 to a comparison group. All 120 pupils take the same reading test at the start and at the end of the term. At the end, 20 pupils in the programme group, all with low start scores, have left the programme and do not take the final test. In the comparison group, 2 pupils are missing. The programme group's average score is higher than the comparison group's.

Which threat to internal validity most directly weakens the conclusion that the programme caused this difference?

A. Selection, because the two groups differed before the programme started.
B. Attrition, because mainly weak readers left the programme group.
C. Testing, because pupils took the same reading test twice.
D. Maturation, because reading skills grow naturally during a term.

### Question 2 (1 pt)
A teacher gives all 90 pupils in year 2 a spelling test. She selects the 12 pupils with the lowest scores and gives them extra support for six weeks. Then these 12 pupils take a different, equally difficult spelling test. Their average score has risen. No other pupils are tested again.

Which threat to internal validity, linked to how these 12 pupils were chosen, could explain part of the rise even if the extra support had no effect?

A. History, because events at school during the six weeks may have helped the pupils.
B. Testing, because the pupils had already done a spelling test before.
C. Selection, because the 12 pupils are not equivalent to the other pupils.
D. Regression to the mean, because pupils with very low scores tend to score closer to average again.

### Question 3 (1 pt)
Researchers recruit 40 first-year psychology students for a study in a quiet university lab. Students are randomly assigned to learn vocabulary with a new flashcard app or with a paper list. Both groups take the same vocabulary test afterwards, and all 40 students complete the study. The app group remembers more words. The researchers conclude that the app will also improve vocabulary learning for secondary-school pupils in busy classrooms.

Which problem most directly limits this conclusion?

A. The results may not generalise to other people and settings.
B. Random assignment may have failed to create equivalent groups.
C. Uneven drop-out may have made the groups different by the end.
D. The measurement of vocabulary may have differed between the groups.

### Question 4 (1 pt)
A school wants to know whether a new feedback method improves essay quality. In October, one teacher scores all pupils' essays with a detailed rubric on a 10-point scale. The method is used for one term. In February, a different teacher scores new essays from the same pupils with a shorter rubric on a 5-point scale. Both sets of scores are converted to percentages. The February percentages are higher.

Which threat to internal validity is created by the way the essays were scored?

A. Testing, because pupils practised writing essays in October.
B. Maturation, because pupils' writing improves naturally over a term.
C. Instrumentation, because the way of scoring changed between the measurements.
D. History, because something else happened at school during the term.

### Question 5 (1 pt)
A researcher wants to know whether a mentoring programme reduced drop-out among the 200 first-year vocational students who took part in a study. A lottery assigns 100 students to mentoring and 100 to no mentoring. Drop-out is recorded for both groups after one year, in the same way.

Which judgement of this design is correct?

A. It cannot answer the question, because there is no pretest to check that the groups were equal.
B. It cannot answer the question, because students who volunteer are not representative of all students.
C. It can answer the question, because random assignment controls selection.
D. It can answer the question only if the groups are first matched on age and gender.

### Question 6 (1 pt)
A municipality introduces a homework-support scheme in all its primary schools in January. An adviser measures the school wellbeing of the same 300 pupils in September and again in June. Wellbeing scores are higher in June. The adviser asks: did the scheme raise pupils' wellbeing?

Which judgement of this design is correct?

A. It can answer the question, because the same pupils are measured twice, so differences between pupils are excluded.
B. It cannot answer the question, because other changes over time are not ruled out by this design.
C. It can answer the question, because the difference between September and June is statistically significant.
D. It cannot answer the question, because two measurements cannot show which came first, scheme or wellbeing.

### Question 7 (1 pt)
A researcher surveys a random sample of 500 pupils from 20 secondary schools. Each pupil reports the number of hours they sleep per night and gives their most recent maths grade. The correlation is positive: pupils who sleep more have higher grades. The researcher asks: does more sleep lead to higher grades?

Which judgement of this design is correct?

A. It can answer the question, because a sample of 500 pupils is large enough to rule out other explanations.
B. It can answer the question, because a positive correlation shows that sleep comes before the grades.
C. It cannot answer the question, because self-reported sleep hours contain error, which makes any causal claim impossible.
D. It cannot answer the question, because the correlation does not show whether sleep affects grades or grades affect sleep.

### Question 8 (1 pt)
A school has two parallel classes. The principal decides that class 3A gets a peer-tutoring programme for one term and class 3B continues as usual. At the end of the term, a researcher gives both classes the same maths test, and 3A scores higher. The researcher wants to answer: did peer tutoring raise maths results? The classes were not formed at random.

Which addition would most improve this design's ability to answer the question?

A. A maths test in both classes before the programme, so that differences at the start can be taken into account.
B. A second maths test in both classes a month after the programme, so that lasting differences can be seen.
C. A questionnaire in class 3A asking pupils whether they found the programme useful.
D. A repeat of the study in another school with the same two-class set-up.

### Question 9 (1 pt)
A researcher wants to know whether a new digital feedback tool improves pupils' writing scores. 120 pupils in one school can take part, and the school lets the researcher decide who uses the tool.

Which design is best able to answer this causal question?

A. Ask all 120 pupils how often they use the tool and correlate this with their writing grades.
B. Let all 120 pupils use the tool and compare their writing scores before and after.
C. Randomly assign 60 pupils to the tool and 60 to usual teaching, then compare writing scores afterwards.
D. Let pupils choose whether to use the tool and compare users with non-users afterwards.

### Question 10 (1 pt)
A researcher measures the exam anxiety of 80 students before and after an eight-week mindfulness course. There is no other group. Anxiety is lower after the course. The researcher wants to be able to say whether the course caused the decrease, separate from other changes over time.

Which change to the design does this best?

A. Measure anxiety with a questionnaire that is more reliable and valid.
B. Add more students to the course group so that the sample is larger.
C. Add a second posttest some weeks after the first posttest.
D. Add a control group that is randomly assigned and measured at the same times.

## Answer model

### Row R1 — Understand (questions 1–4)

#### Question 1
**Correct answer:** B. The weakest readers left only the programme group, so the remaining programme pupils score higher on average because of who stayed. This is differential drop-out, which is attrition.
**A:** Wrong because pupils were randomly assigned, so the groups were equivalent at the start. The distractor catches students who see unequal groups at the end and call it selection.
**C:** Wrong because both groups took the same test twice, so any testing effect applies to both groups and does not explain the difference. It catches students who name a threat that is present in the case but is not the main one.
**D:** Wrong because natural growth during the term affects both groups. It catches students who name maturation for any change over time.

#### Question 2
**Correct answer:** D. The 12 pupils were chosen for their extreme low scores, so they are likely to score closer to average on a retest without any effect of the support.
**A:** Wrong because history is not tied to how the pupils were chosen, and the case gives no sign of such an event. It catches students who name history for any change over time without a control group.
**B:** Wrong because the retest used a different, equally difficult test, which removes the effect of repeating the same test. It catches students who think any retest causes a testing effect.
**C:** Wrong because selection concerns non-equivalent groups that are compared. No comparison is made here, and selection does not create a rise on its own. It catches a mix-up between selecting extreme pupils (regression) and non-equivalent groups (selection).

#### Question 3
**Correct answer:** A. The sample (first-year psychology students) and the setting (quiet lab) differ from the target (secondary-school pupils in busy classrooms), which is a threat to external validity.
**B:** Wrong because random assignment controls selection, so the groups were equivalent at the start. It catches the misconception that randomisation can fail by definition or is not enough.
**C:** Wrong because all 40 students completed the study, so there was no drop-out. It catches students who pick an internal threat from the list.
**D:** Wrong because both groups took the same vocabulary test, so measurement did not change. It catches students who pick an internal threat from the list.

#### Question 4
**Correct answer:** C. Different scorers, rubrics and scales were used in October and February, so a change in measurement may explain the difference. This is instrumentation.
**A:** Wrong because the case describes a change in scoring, not an effect of the earlier measurement. It catches students who name testing for any repeated measurement.
**B:** Wrong because maturation is a real threat in this one-group design, but it is not created by the way the essays were scored, which is what the question asks.
**D:** Wrong because history is a general threat in this design, but it is not created by the way the essays were scored, which is what the question asks.

### Row R2 — Evaluate (questions 5–10)

#### Question 5
**Correct answer:** C. Random assignment (the lottery) controls selection, so the design supports a causal claim about the students who took part.
**A:** Wrong because randomisation makes the groups equivalent without needing a pretest to establish it. It catches the belief that a pretest is always required for a causal claim.
**B:** Wrong because representativeness concerns external validity (generalising), not whether the effect among these students is caused by the programme. The question is about the participating students only. It catches a mix-up of internal and external validity.
**D:** Wrong because random assignment already controls selection, so matching is not needed. It catches the belief that groups must be matched in addition to randomisation.

#### Question 6
**Correct answer:** B. A one-group pretest–posttest design cannot rule out history, maturation and regression to the mean, so it cannot show that the scheme raised wellbeing.
**A:** Wrong because measuring the same pupils twice does not rule out events or natural change between the two measurements. It catches the belief that using the same persons solves all validity problems.
**C:** Wrong because statistical significance shows that a difference is unlikely to be chance, not what caused it. It catches a mix-up of statistical significance and causal inference.
**D:** Wrong because the scheme started before the June measurement, so the order of events is known. The problem is the alternative explanations. It catches a mix-up with the correlational design, which cannot establish direction.

#### Question 7
**Correct answer:** D. A correlational design cannot establish the direction of an effect, so grades could also influence sleep.
**A:** Wrong because sample size does not control for explanations or establish direction. It catches the belief that a large sample makes a causal claim possible.
**B:** Wrong because a correlation does not show which variable comes first. It catches the belief that a strong correlation implies causation.
**C:** Wrong because measurement error makes results less precise but does not make every causal claim impossible, and it is not the weakness the material names for this design. It catches a mix-up with instrumentation and an overstated claim about measurement error.

#### Question 8
**Correct answer:** A. A quasi-experiment with non-equivalent groups needs a pretest and control for selection, so a pretest in both classes lets the researcher take the differences at the start into account.
**B:** Wrong because a later test shows whether the difference lasts but does not address the non-equivalent classes. It catches students who add more measurements instead of controlling selection.
**C:** Wrong because opinions of pupils in one class do not show the programme's effect on results and do not control selection. It catches students who accept satisfaction as evidence of effect.
**D:** Wrong because repeating the same set-up repeats the selection problem. At best it relates to generalisation. It catches a mix-up of replication or external validity with internal validity.

#### Question 9
**Correct answer:** C. A randomised controlled trial supports causal claims best, because random assignment controls selection, and here the researcher can decide who uses the tool.
**A:** Wrong because a correlational design cannot establish the direction of an effect. It catches the belief that correlating use with grades answers a causal question.
**B:** Wrong because a one-group pretest–posttest design cannot rule out history, maturation and regression to the mean. It catches the belief that a before–after difference shows the effect.
**D:** Wrong because pupils who choose to use the tool may differ from those who do not, so selection is not controlled. It catches the belief that having a comparison group is enough.

#### Question 10
**Correct answer:** D. A randomly assigned control group measured at the same times faces the same history, maturation and regression, so the course effect can be separated from other changes over time.
**A:** Wrong because a better questionnaire improves measurement but does not separate the course effect from other changes over time. It catches the belief that measurement quality solves design problems.
**B:** Wrong because a larger sample does not control history, maturation or regression. It catches the belief that more participants strengthen a causal claim.
**C:** Wrong because a second posttest adds a measurement but no comparison, so other changes over time are still not ruled out. It catches the belief that more measurements in one group can show causation.

Correct answers by position: A = 2 (questions 3, 8), B = 2 (questions 1, 6), C = 3 (questions 4, 5, 9), D = 3 (questions 2, 7, 10).

Remarks:
- I found no error in the blueprint.
- Coverage in R1: four questions cannot cover all seven internal threats plus external validity. The correct answers cover attrition, regression to the mean, external validity and instrumentation. Selection, history, maturation and testing appear as distractors only.
- Coverage in R2: randomised controlled trial (questions 5, 9), quasi-experiment with non-equivalent groups (question 8), one-group pretest–posttest (questions 6, 10), correlational design (question 7).

## Self-check

- **Does every multiple-choice question have exactly one correct answer?** Yes, because each case rules out the other options with facts in the stem (for example random assignment, a different equivalent test, full completion) or with the material (for example direction in correlational designs).
- **Is there no clue to the correct answer anywhere?** Yes, because I kept the options in each question alike in length and form, and the correct answers are spread over A to D.
- **Are all distractors plausible?** Yes, because each one is a known mix-up, such as internal versus external validity, pretest–posttest versus correlational, or a large sample versus control of selection.
- **Does every question test the cognitive level of its row?** Yes, because questions 1–4 ask students to classify a threat in a new case (Understand) and questions 5–10 ask for a judgement of a design against causal inference in a new case (Evaluate).
- **Does everything follow from the material?** Yes, because all threats, designs and judgements come from the material, and all case data are fictitious and given in full in each question.
- **Does any question give away the answer to another?** No, because each case is separate, and the one-group design in questions 6 and 10 is approached from different sides without naming the control-group solution in question 6.
